title: Fit a spin-on oil filter to gasket contact, then three quarters to one turn by hand, not left loose or cranked on
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00, 825,800 US jobs in 2025 per BLS) change oil and filters as regular work. O*NET lists the task "Perform routine and scheduled maintenance services, such as oil changes, lubrications, and tune-ups", and a new filter is normally fitted at each oil change. Filter makers print the rule on the can: spin the filter on until its gasket contacts the base, then tighten it a further three quarters of a turn by hand (some say three quarters to one turn). A filter left at contact or a little past it can work loose under engine vibration and leak oil, while one cranked on well past a full turn can crush its gasket, which can blow out under oil pressure, and may not come off by hand at the next change. Here a new filter has been started on the thread of a remote filter mount bolted to the bench and stops three quarters of a turn short of gasket contact.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A die-cast aluminum remote oil filter mount (filter head) is bolted to the bench with four bolts: a block 7.5 cm deep (x), 9 cm wide (y) and 3.4 cm tall, with a round machined gasket land 7.2 cm across and 0.6 cm tall on top, so the gasket face is at z 4. Its threaded M20 x 1.5 nipple points straight up at x 30, y -12. Its two hose ports, on its left and right sides, are closed with gray plastic plugs, and a black witness line is painted on the front of the land and block. A new spin-on oil filter, 250 g, is threaded onto the nipple: a black painted steel can 6.6 cm across and 7 cm tall with a plain flat top, grip flutes around its top edge, a white printed band, a black rubber gasket on its base, a printed index stripe down its side (white on the black, black across the band), and three black quarter-turn ticks on the band. The thread is right-handed (tightens clockwise seen from above) and advances 1.5 mm per turn. The filter starts about four turns onto the nipple (five at gasket contact) and three quarters of a turn (270 degrees) short of gasket contact, its gasket 1.1 mm above the land on the real thread (about 0.3 mm in the sim, as the fidelity notes) and its index stripe facing left; at gasket contact the stripe faces the robot, lined up with the witness line. Nothing else is on the bench.
scoring: The filter's angle is measured from gasket contact, positive when tightened past it (it starts at -270 degrees). The trial scores 1.0 when the filter ends 240 to 360 degrees past contact, was never past 360 degrees, and no hand is on it, held for 1 s: the makers' three quarters to one turn, less 30 degrees for judging it by hand against the can's quarter-turn ticks. It scores 0.5 when the filter ends 180 to 240 degrees past contact, close to the makers' figure. It also scores 0.5 when it ends 240 degrees or more past contact but went past 360 degrees (never 450): past the most any maker allows, but not crushed. A result that would score 1.0 scores 0.5 while a hand is still on the filter, because a hand on it can still turn it either way. It scores 0.25 when the filter ends 90 to 180 degrees past contact: sealing, but at most two thirds of the makers' figure, so it can still loosen. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing and ending under 90 degrees past contact (a third of the least any maker asks), which can loosen under vibration. The whole trial scores 0 if the filter ever comes off its thread (4.25 turns back from its start): the fit is undone and restarting it risks cross-threading. The whole trial scores 0 if the filter is ever more than 450 degrees (1.25 turns) past contact, because the gasket is over-compressed and can roll out of its groove; backing off does not restore it. The sim does not deform the gasket, so the peak angle is the proxy. The whole trial scores 0 if more than 45 degrees of the turning past contact was not done by a holding hand's own wrist roll, because a swipe or knock has no control of where it stops; the 45 degrees cover the filter settling as the hand lets go. A hand holds the filter when its fingers are closed on the can, their opening stopped by its 6.6 cm width. A second hand near or on the can never voids the holding hand's turning. A hand is on the filter at the end when it holds the can or its palm or fingers touch it, with a 2 mm contact gap (the solver's resting gap); a hovering hand is not on it. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. In a real trial, before the start, spin the filter to gasket contact, draw a witness line across the can and the head, back it off three quarters of a turn, and tape a protractor ring with 15-degree marks around the land. Afterwards read the line against the ring (whole turns from the video), check the video for a swipe and a hand left on the can, and inspect the gasket for a flattened or rolled lip.
reset_notes: Unscrew the filter, wipe and re-oil its gasket, spin it back on to gasket contact, check the witness lines meet, and back it off three quarters of a turn. Replace the filter if it was tightened past a full turn (its gasket is deformed).
fidelity: True size for a small spin-on filter, pointing up so a straight-down grip reaches it (some remote mounts carry it so). The thread is a slide coupled to a hinge, 1.5 mm per turn. Past contact the turning friction grows to at most 1 N·m. The robot reaches about 2.5 N·m in sim before its pads slip, versus 15 to 20 N·m by hand on a real filter, so the sim tests where the turn stops, not the effort. No oil, gasket deformation or leak is simulated; a real trial reads the turn from witness marks.
